questions.q: The words "SOCIALIST," "SECULAR," and "INTEGRITY" were inserted into the Preamble by which Amendment?
questions.src: The 42nd Amendment Act 1976, often called the "Mini-Constitution," inserted these words into the Preamble.

questions.q: Article 19(1) of the Constitution guarantees how many distinct freedoms?
questions.src: Article 19(1) guarantees six freedoms: speech/expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession/trade/business.

questions.q: The grounds of prohibited discrimination under Article 15(1) are:
o: Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, and age
Religion, race, caste, sex, and place of birth
Religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, and residence
questions.src: Article 15(1) lists exactly five grounds — religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth — and notably does NOT include age or residence.

questions.q: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), the Supreme Court held that "procedure established by law" under Article 21 must be:
o: Simply any procedure enacted by a competent legislature, regardless of fairness
FAIR, JUST, and REASONABLE, not merely enacted
Only applicable to citizens, never foreigners
questions.src: Maneka Gandhi read substantive due process into Article 21, requiring the procedure itself to be fair, just, and reasonable.

questions.q: Article 21A (Right to Education) was inserted by which Amendment, and covers which age group?
questions.src: The 86th Amendment 2002 inserted Article 21A, guaranteeing free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14.

questions.q: A person arrested must be produced before the nearest Magistrate within how many hours under Article 22?
questions.src: Article 22 requires production before a Magistrate within 24 hours, excluding the time necessary for travel from the place of arrest.

questions.q: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar referred to which Article as "the heart and soul of the Constitution"?
questions.src: Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) was famously described by Ambedkar in these terms.

questions.q: The Directive Principles of State Policy (Part IV) are:
o: Fully enforceable by courts, exactly like Fundamental Rights
NON-JUSTICIABLE, yet declared fundamental in the governance of the country under Article 37
Only applicable during a national emergency
questions.src: DPSPs are expressly non-justiciable under Article 37, though declared fundamental to governance.

questions.q: The writ of "Certiorari" is used to:
o: Prevent a proceeding before it concludes
QUASH a decision already made by a subordinate court/tribunal acting without or in excess of jurisdiction
Compel performance of a public duty
Challenge unlawful occupation of public office
questions.src: Certiorari is corrective — it quashes an already-made decision, distinct from Prohibition's preventive function.

questions.q: Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction), compared to Article 32 (Supreme Court), is generally:
o: WIDER — covering Fundamental Rights AND "any other purpose"
Not applicable to Fundamental Rights at all
questions.src: Article 226's "any other purpose" language gives it broader scope than Article 32.

questions.q: The word "internal disturbance" in Article 352 was replaced with "armed rebellion" by which Amendment?
questions.src: The 44th Amendment 1978, responding to the 1975 Emergency's misuse, made this change.

questions.q: "Financial Emergency" under Article 360, in India's constitutional history to date, has been:
questions.src: Article 360 remains a purely theoretical provision, never formally proclaimed in India.

questions.q: Under Article 368, amendments affecting the federal structure (e.g., Article 368 itself, Presidential election) require:
o: Special majority PLUS ratification by at least one-half of State Legislatures
Only Presidential assent, no Parliamentary vote
questions.src: This third, most stringent amendment mode protects genuinely federal-structure-affecting provisions.

questions.q: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Basic Structure Doctrine was established by a bench of how many judges, with what majority?
questions.src: This remains the largest Constitution Bench in Indian history, deciding by a narrow 7:6 majority.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly represents the chronological sequence of the Basic Structure case law?
o: Kesavananda Bharati → Golaknath → Shankari Prasad → Minerva Mills
Shankari Prasad → Golaknath → Kesavananda Bharati → Minerva Mills
Minerva Mills → Kesavananda Bharati → Golaknath → Shankari Prasad
Golaknath → Shankari Prasad → Minerva Mills → Kesavananda Bharati
questions.src: The correct chronological sequence is Shankari Prasad (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda Bharati (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980).

questions.q: The Ninth Schedule, which shields specified laws from Fundamental-Rights-based judicial review, was added by:
questions.src: The Ninth Schedule was added by the very first constitutional amendment in 1951.

questions.q: Following I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007), laws placed in the Ninth Schedule are:
o: Completely immune from judicial review under all circumstances
STILL reviewable if they damage the Constitution's Basic Structure
questions.src: I.R. Coelho clarified that Ninth Schedule protection does not extend to laws that violate the Basic Structure.

questions.q: The Tenth Schedule, dealing with Anti-Defection provisions, was added by which Amendment?
questions.src: The 52nd Amendment 1985 inserted the Tenth Schedule governing disqualification for defection.

questions.q: The Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules, dealing with Panchayat and Municipality powers respectively, were added by:
questions.src: The 73rd Amendment (Panchayats, Eleventh Schedule) and 74th Amendment (Municipalities, Twelfth Schedule), both 1992, established constitutional status for local self-government.

questions.q: The minimum age to be eligible for election as President of India is:
questions.src: Article 58 sets the minimum age qualification for the Presidency at 35 years.

questions.q: Supreme Court judges retire upon attaining the age of:
questions.src: Supreme Court judges have a retirement age of 65, distinct from High Court judges' retirement age of 62.

questions.q: High Court judges retire upon attaining the age of:
questions.src: High Court judges retire at 62, while Supreme Court judges retire at 65 — a frequently tested distinguishing pair.

questions.q: The National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), introduced by the 99th Amendment 2014, was:
o: Upheld as constitutional and remains in force today
STRUCK DOWN in 2015 (Fourth Judges Case), preserving the Collegium system
Never brought before the Supreme Court
Replaced by a fully executive-controlled appointment system
questions.src: The Fourth Judges Case (2015) struck down the NJAC as violating judicial independence, a Basic Structure feature.

questions.q: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992), the Supreme Court, while upholding OBC reservation, introduced which important ceiling?
questions.src: The 50% reservation ceiling (with limited later-recognised exceptions) is one of Indra Sawhney's most cited holdings.

questions.q: Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer is generally credited as:
o: The first Chief Justice of independent India
The father of Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India
The chairman of the Constituent Assembly Drafting Committee
questions.src: Justice Krishna Iyer is widely regarded as the pioneering figure behind PIL in India, with Justice P.N. Bhagwati also central to its development.

questions.q: In Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a 9-judge bench of the Supreme Court held that:
o: Right to Privacy is not protected by the Constitution
Right to Privacy IS a Fundamental Right under Article 21
Right to Privacy applies only to public figures
Right to Privacy was left undecided
questions.src: This landmark 9-judge bench ruling firmly established privacy as a Fundamental Right flowing from Article 21.

questions.q: The "Doctrine of Pith and Substance" is used by courts to:
o: Determine the punishment for a criminal offence
Determine the TRUE NATURE of a law when it appears to touch subjects in different Legislative Lists
Calculate compensation in land acquisition cases
questions.src: This doctrine examines a law's true character/substance to determine which legislature validly enacted it, rather than its incidental effects.

questions.q: The "Doctrine of Colourable Legislation" is based on the principle that:
o: A legislature can do indirectly what it cannot do directly, without restriction
What CANNOT be done directly CANNOT be done indirectly — examining legislative competence, not motive
Only the judiciary can enact colourable legislation
It applies exclusively to Money Bills
questions.src: This doctrine focuses on whether a legislature had the constitutional competence to enact a law, regardless of its stated purpose.

questions.q: In Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court:
o: Upheld Section 377 IPC in its entirety
Read down Section 377 IPC, decriminalising consensual homosexual acts between adults
Struck down the entire Indian Penal Code
Declined to address the constitutional question
questions.src: This landmark ruling decriminalised consensual same-sex relations between adults by reading down Section 377.

questions.q: In Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), the Supreme Court held that the Right to a SPEEDY TRIAL is:
o: Not part of any constitutional right
Part of the Right to Life and Personal Liberty under Article 21
Only applicable to civil cases, never criminal
A statutory right under the CrPC only, with no constitutional basis
questions.src: This landmark case, concerning undertrial prisoners, established speedy trial as a facet of Article 21.
